title: Santa's sleigh will be weighed down by tariffs
gist: Tariffs on sports gear, art supplies, instruments and consoles rose from ~5% to 20-28% effective rates in 2025 and remain 14-17% after the Supreme Court ruling. Imports fell 17-33%, prices keep rising faster than core goods, and no manufacturing revival has materialized.

themes.theme: Tariff rate surge on hobby goods

insights.claim: Effective US tariff rates on sports equipment, pencils/crayons and musical instruments were 5.6%, 5.0% and 5.7% in the 2024 holiday season (Sep-Dec).
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Baseline shows scale of 2025 tariff shock on consumer discretionary imports.

insights.claim: By the 2025 holiday season effective tariff rates jumped to 27.7% on sports equipment, 26.6% on pencils and crayons and 21.2% on instruments, driven by the escalated trade war with China where most are made.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Heavy China exposure in low-end consumer goods drove the peak.

insights.claim: After the Supreme Court struck down some tariffs, effective rates through August 2026 eased only to 17.2% (sports equipment), 16.1% (pencils/crayons) and 14.1% (instruments), still roughly 3x the 2024 levels.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Tariff relief is partial; a structurally higher tariff floor persists.

themes.theme: Demand destruction rather than import substitution

insights.claim: Holiday-season imports in 2025 fell 24% for musical instruments and 17% each for sports equipment and pencils/crayons versus 2024.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Volume contraction hits importers and retailers of discretionary goods.

insights.claim: Higher prices did not shift buyers to domestic producers because entry-level versions of these products largely are not made in the US; the tariffs instead destroyed demand.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Tariffs on goods with no domestic substitute act as pure consumption taxes.

insights.claim: Trump's tariffs have not produced a US manufacturing boom in either employment or construction.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Undercuts the reshoring rationale for the tariffs.

insights.claim: Prices for all three goods classes rose in 2026 relative to 2025 and have outpaced core goods prices since 2024, even as tariffs eased.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Retail margins and prices ratchet up; tariff relief is not a disinflation channel.

insights.claim: Three reasons prices stay high: importers sold pre-tariff stock in 2025 so 2026 prices reflect tariffs that held until the February 2026 Supreme Court decision; retail prices rise fast and fall slowly; and underlying inflation remains elevated.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Pass-through is asymmetric, so tariff cuts help margins before consumers.

insights.claim: Core consumer prices are up 5.7% over two years, stoked by spillovers from the war with Iran and large fiscal deficits, further eroding purchasing power.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Elevated core inflation forces households to cut wants versus needs.

insights.claim: Musical instrument prices rose 9.1% over the period versus 2.3% for core goods, so general inflation cannot explain the increase; instruments saw the steepest price rise and largest import drop.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Tariff-exposed categories show much larger price gains than the core goods index.

insights.claim: Importers of record are receiving tariff refunds, but little is likely to be passed to consumers who ultimately paid.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Refund windfalls may accrue to importers and retailers.

insights.claim: Video game console effective tariff rates went from zero in the 2024 holiday season to 19.7% in 2025, with calculated duties rising from nothing to $508 million.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Consoles are a meaningful duty base.

insights.claim: Console imports spiked in early 2025 on front-running and the Nintendo Switch 2 launch, then fell 33% over the 2025 holiday season; through August 2026 they were 10% below 2024 levels.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Front-loading pulled forward demand, followed by a payback slump.

insights.claim: Console list prices kept rising: PS5 went from $499.99 to $549.99 in August 2025 and $649.99 in April 2026; Xbox Series X from $499.99 to $799.99 in three steps between May 2025 and August 2026; Switch 2 rose $50 in September.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Hardware makers are passing through cost and raising list prices repeatedly.

themes.theme: Second-order effects on domestic industry and society

insights.claim: Cheap imported beginner gear feeds rather than competes with US manufacturing, since kids who learn on starter instruments become buyers of premium US-made brands such as Gibson or Ludwig.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Tariffs on entry-level goods may erode future premium domestic demand.
insights.quote: Cheap imported beginner gear doesn't so much compete with American manufacturing as feed it

insights.claim: Firms like Trek and Wilson split production, making entry-level lines abroad and high-end lines in the US, consistent with research showing offshoring firms keep making the same goods at home, upgrade quality and shift toward technology jobs.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Blanket tariffs ignore the split-production model of US brands.

insights.claim: School music, art and athletic programs buy on fixed budgets, so tariffs reduce gear available, and low-income families who depend on those programs are hit first.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Tariffs have regressive effects and cut into human capital formation.

insights.claim: The administration has granted firm-specific tariff relief to producers of many other products, but not to goods that build skills in children.
insights.speaker: Cullen S. Hendrix
insights.so_what: Signals tariff relief is selective and politically negotiated.
